stem: A study comparing the clinical benefi ts a new drug X with placebo consists of two arms. Following randomisation, both control group and treatment group contains 100 patients each. Unfortunately only, 80 patients agreed to take drug X in the treatment group due to various reasons. Which of the following is the best course of action?

The study is invalid because not all patients participated.
The study must be reviewed again by the ethics committee before proceeding

correctAnswer: All patients should be included in the analysis.

stem: A study looked at whether poverty and unemployment increases the risk of common mental illnesses or delays the recovery. Adults aged 16-75 living in private households were chosen for the study. Outcomes were assessed using the General Health Questionnaire (GHQ). Data was used from the British Household Panel Survey. 10,264 individuals aged 16-75 participated in the survey at the start of the study (Time 1). The GHQ was completed by 9,064 individuals (94.3% of those interviewed) at Time 1. Of these 9,064 subjects, 7,726 (85.2%) were re- interviewed a year later (Time 2). Common mental disorders were assessed using the GHQ as a single domain. A score of 3 or more on the GHQ was used to confi rm cases. 1024 cases with common mental illness were observed (686 employed, 58 unemployed and 285 economically inactive) while 4837 remained as non-cases (3102 employed, 204 unemployed and 1531 economically inactive). Poverty was scored as one point each for various indicators of poor income and living conditions. Financial strain at Time 1 was assessed by asking recording one of three ordinal responses to a single question. Results of the study indicated that non-participation was associated with low socio-economic status at both sets of interviews. Compared with 1% of the 1991 census, those living in very large households and households with no car or van were under represented to a statistically signifi cant degree. Loss to follow-up was associated with a higher mean poverty score (P=0.0001) but not withfi nancial strain (p=0.027). Use the attached table to answer the questions. A particular strength of the external validity of this study is:
options: High level of GHQ completion at Time 1.
explanation: As the sampling frame represents the majority of those living in Britain, external validity is very good for this study.

stem: A study was conducted to test alleged association between creativity and psychopathology and to investigate whether any such association is the result of environmental or genetic factors (Kyaga et al., Br J Psychiatry. 2011 Nov;199(5):373-9.). Index subjects were identifi ed from a Hospital Discharge Register (National Board of Health and Welfare) that provided discharge diagnoses for all in-patient treatment episodes for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and unipolar depression in Sweden between 1973 and 2003. The Multi-Generation Register (Statistics Sweden) enables identifi cation of biological relatives of an index person, including all individuals born in Sweden since 1932 and whoever registered as living in Sweden after 1960. Ten individuals matched on gender and birth year were randomly selected as controls from the Multi-Generation Register for each index person in the case group and each of their relatives; controls had to be alive, within the country, and without any in-patient episode for the studied disorder at the date of thefi rst hospitalisation of the individual in the case group. National censuses (Statistics Sweden) based on mandatory self-report questionnaires completed by all adult citizens in 1960, 1970, 1980 and 1990 provided information on professions in the entire Swedish population. The likelihood of holding a creative occupation in individuals who had received in-patient treatment for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or unipolar depression and their relatives without such a diagnosis was compared with that of controls. Results suggested that individuals with bipolar disorder and healthy siblings of people with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder were overrepresented in creative professions. People with schizophrenia had no increased rate of overall creative professions compared with controls, but an increased rate in the subgroup of artistic occupations. Neither individuals with unipolar depression nor their siblings diff ered from controls regarding creative professions. A familial cosegregation of both schizophrenia and bipolar disorder with creativity is suggested. What type of study design has been used?
explanation: This study used a nested case-control design using longitudinal Swedish total population registers. Registers help to identify cohorts with longitudinal data being available. From these cohorts, cases (2 types: patients and relatives) and controls have been selected. So this is a nested design.

stem: Antipsychotic Drugs and Hyperglycemia in Older Patients With Diabetes Background: Evidence suggests that there is an association between antipsychotic drugs and new-onset diabetes, but little is known about the risk of hyperglycaemia among persons with pre-existing diabetes. Methods: Using population-based health databases in Ontario, Canada, persons aged 66 years or older with diabetes who started treatment with an antipsychotic drug from April 1, 2002, to March 31, 2006, were followed up from treatment start until March 31, 2007. The cohort was subdivided into 3 groups: insulin-treated, an oral hypoglycaemic agent only -treated, and no diabetes treatment. We defi ned cases as patients hospitalized (emergency department visit or hospital admissions) for hyperglycaemia. Each case was matched with up to 10 controls for age, sex, year of cohort entry and duration of follow-up. The authors compared the likelihood of hyperglycaemia among current users of atypical and typical antipsychotic agents with that among remote antipsychotic users (discontinued >180 days), based on prescriptions closest to the event date. Results: Of 13 817 patients studied, 1515 (11.0%) were hospitalized for hyperglycaemia. Current antipsychotic treatment was associated with a higher risk of hyperglycaemia compared with remote antipsychotic use in all diabetes treatment groups (overall adjusted rate ratio, 1.50; 95% confi dence interval, 1.29-1.74). The risk was increased among patients who were treated with atypical and typical antipsychotic agents and was extremely high among patients who were just starting treatment (only 1 prescription before event). Conclusions: Among older patients with diabetes, the initiation of treatment with antipsychotic drugs was associated with a signifi cantly increased risk of hospitalization for hyperglycaemia (P < .001). The risk was particularly high during the initial course of treatment and was increased with the use of all antipsychotic agents. Ref: Lipscombe et al., Arch Intern Med. 2009;169(14):1282-1289 The study cohort has been defi ned as
options: Diabetic individuals older than 66 years living in Ontario and started on antipsychotics between 2002 and 2006
Diabetic individuals older than 66 years living in Ontario and treated using either insulin, oral hypoglycaemic agent or on no treatment
Diabetic individuals older than 66 years living in Ontario and hospitalized for hyperglycaemia
Individuals older than 66 years living in Ontario and started on antipsychotics between 2002 and 2006, irrespective of diabetic status
Diabetic individuals older than 66 years living in Ontario and exposed to antipsychotics anytime in their lives
correctAnswer: Diabetic individuals older than 66 years living in Ontario and started on antipsychotics between 2002 and 2006
explanation: Persons living in Ontario, aged 66 years or older with diabetes who started treatment with an antipsychotic drug from April 1, 2002, to March 31, 2006, were followed up from treatment start until March 31, 2007. They form the original cohort.

explanation: GHB: Abused for euphoric eff ects that are short lived - called Georgia Home Boy. Used as a substitute for ecstasy in dance parties (raves) - called liquid ecstasy. stem: Which of the following physiological changes often produce an artifi cially elevated calcium level in blood?
explanation: Only one half of the exchangeable calcium in blood is in the active ionized form with the remainder bound to albumin, globulin, and other inorganic molecules. Protein binding of calcium is infl uenced by pH with metabolic acidosis leading to increased ionized calcium from reduced protein binding, and alkalosis leading to reduced ionized calcium from increased protein binding. Because calcium binds to albumin and only the unbound (free or ionized) calcium is biologically active, the serum level must be adjusted for abnormal albumin levels. For every 1-g/dL drop in serum albumin below 4 g/dL, measured serum calcium decreases by 0.8 mg/dL. Therefore, to correct for an albumin level of less than 4 g/dL, one should add 0.8 to the measured value of calcium for each 1-g/dL decrease in albumin. Without this correction, an abnormally high serum calcium level may appear to be normal. (From http://emedicine.medscape.com/article/240681-overview)

stem: Which of the following antidepressant must be avoided in a patient with breast cancer taking tamoxifen?
explanation: Paroxetine,fl uoxetine, duloxetine and bupropion are strong CYP2D6 inhibitors, which should be avoided in tamoxifen users. Amitriptyline and its metabolite, nortriptyline, are metabolized by and can inhibit CYP2D6. Fluvoxamine and nefazodone both inhibit CYP3A, which could potentially aff ect the metabolism of tamoxifen. Venlafaxine has little or no eff ect on the metabolism of tamoxifen and may be considered the safest choice of antidepressants. Mirtazapine has not been extensively studied, but existing research suggests minimal eff ect on CYP2D6. The remaining commonly prescribed antidepressants have mild to moderate degrees of CYP2D6 inhibition. (Excerpt retrieved from Desmaraias & Looper 2010 http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20141708 )

Erectile and orgasmic dysfunctions are less common with Mirtazapine. (Ref: Ozmenler NK et al. Mirtazapine augmentation in depressed patients with sexual dysfunction due to SSRIs, Hum psychopharmacology 2008; 23: 321-326)

stem: The most common psychiatric presentation among the following conditions that is seen in those with cancer is
explanation: Prevalence of major depression in those with advanced cancer is about 5 –15%. About 10 –15% of cancer patients present with less severe symptoms. The prevalence of depression in advanced disease is closer to 33% (Hotopf et al. 2001). Somatic symptoms are not useful when diagnosing depression in the physically ill. Pervasive global anhedonia is a more valid criterion for the diagnosis of depression.

stem: The most commonly admitted hallucinatory experience among respondents of general population surveys in UK is

Vision of Angel or God while going to sleep
External voices speaking in meaningful sentences
correctAnswer: Hearing or seeing things that no one else could experience
explanation: Proportion of general population with highly specifi c hallucinatory experience such as voices is very low.

stem: The one-week prevalence of generalized anxiety disorder according to National Psychiatric Morbidity Survey is
explanation: The one week prevalence of generalized anxiety disorder according to National psychiatric morbidity survey is 3.1%

stem: Which of the following is indicative of epileptic rather than non-epilepticfi ts?
explanation: Psychogenic non-epileptic attacks are often precipitated by stressful circumstances and in response to suggestion. They may occur in wakefulness and in the presence of witnesses and lack stereotypic patterns (asynchronous, asymmetrical, waxing and waning, often with pelvic thrusts,fl ailing and tremors). These may be interrupted or resistant to restraint. Attempts to open the eyes passively often result in tightening of the eyelids. Consciousness may be retained throughout and there is often no actual postictal confusion. The patient may become emotional and cry after the end of the nonepileptic seizure. After a generalised tonic clonic seizure the corneal refl ex will usually be impaired and plantar responses extensor. These are commonly absent in nonepileptic seizures. (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK2609/)

stem: Which of the following antipsychotic drug is most likely to cause orthostatic hypotension?
explanation: Risperidone can cause signifi cantfi rst-dose orthostatic hypotension which can recur every time during a dose increase.

stem: Which of the following rating scales includes a physical examination?
explanation: SAS is a scale for assessing extra pyramidal symptoms - hence it requires a physical examination to be completed.

stem: A 36-year-old man with a history of alcohol dependent syndrome is clinically depressed. What is the drug of choice?
explanation: If a patient has problem-drinking pattern with alcohol and feels suicidal, SSRIs like sertraline are better tolerated and are generally thought to be safer than, for example, tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), especially due to accidental overdose risk. In addition, the frequency of adverse eff ects is relatively low, and the severity of most adverse eff ects is mild or moderate.

stem: Tom is a 7-year-old boy with autistic spectrum disorder. He suff ers from insomnia. The drug of choice is;
explanation: All forms of insomnia are more common in children with learning diffi culties, autism, ADHD and sensory impairments (esp. visual). Although behavioural interventions should be the primary intervention and have a robust evidence base, exogenous melatonin is now the 'fi rst-line' medication prescribed for childhood insomnia. (Ref: The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines- 10th edition-pg 279)

stem: Lucy is a 6-year-old girl who isfi ne at home and mute in school. The diagnosis is:
explanation: Elective mutism is a condition in which children demonstrate normal language skills in some situations but fail to speak in others. Typically, the child speaks with familiar people in familiar surroundings. Eg at home, but fails to speak at school or with strangers.

stem: John is a 12-year-old boy with autism and with severe behavioural disturbances. He has been reported as aggressive and violent to caregivers. The treatment of choice is
explanation: There is now reasonable evidence for the use of risperidone in the management of aggression, tantrums and self-injury in autistic spectrum disorder. (Ref: Oxford Handbook of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry- 139)

stem: A child with Tourette's disorder has had signifi cant weight gain on previous treatment. Which of the following should be off ered?
explanation: Weight gain may be more pronounced in children and adolescents than in adults, and this may limit the use of atypicals in young people. Though there is no established evidence, available case series suggest Aripiprazole is eff ective and well tolerated in children with tics & Tourette's syndrome. (Ref: The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines- 10th edition-pg 277)

stem: A 17-year-old girl with a history of anorexia nervosa has a BMI of 14, blood pressure of 80/40 mm Hg and has reported two episodes of fainting. Where will you treat her?
explanation: BMI less than 14, BP less than 80/60 mm Hg, pulse rate less than 40 beats per minute in patients with anorexia suggests 'high-risk' and such patients should receive immediate medical treatment. Where there is a choice between medical or psychiatric admission, medical admission is preferred where risk of feeding syndrome is high and BMI low, allowing more frequent physical monitoring and more immediate advanced resuscitation facilities than might be available on an eating disorders ward in a psychiatric setting.

stem: The annual risk of a healthcare professional being stalked by a patient or a patient's relative is
explanation: The risk of being stalked by a patient or a patient's relative is between 5% and 10% in a year, and around 20% over the course of a career (Purcell et al, 2005; Mullen et al, 2009). Several surveys of health professionals (summarised by the RCPsych: Retrieved from http://www.rcpsych.ac.uk/workinpsychiatry/psychiatristssupportservice/information) suggest that around 5-11% have been stalked, using a strict operational defi nition, in a year. There is some variation depending on profession and also within psychiatric subspecialties: for example, forensic psychiatrists and general adult psychiatrists appear to be at higher risk, whereas the risk seems to be lower for old age psychiatrists and neuropsychiatrists. (Ref: Royal College of Psychiatrists-2010; Document on Support Service for Psychiatrists). http://bjp.rcpsych.org/content/188/5/403.full

stem: What is the relative risk of psychosis in prisons compared to general population?
explanation: Prisoners were several times (nearly 20 times) more likely to have psychosis and major depression, and about ten times more likely to have antisocial personality disorder, than the general population (Retrieved from http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11867106).

stem: In order to diagnose antisocial personality disorder, DSM-5 requires evidence for antisocial behaviour pattern before the age of
explanation: Evidence of conduct disorder before the age of 15 is required by the DSM-5.

stem: How many homicide off enders have active psychiatric symptoms at the time of committing homicide?
explanation: Shaw (2006) determined 34% of homicides are related to the mental disorder and 5% of homicides are linked to schizophrenia; 10% of homicide off enders have active symptoms at the time of the off ence.

stem: In the UK the number of infanticides reported per year is around
explanation: Under the 1938 Infanticide Act, a woman who kills her child when it is less than a year old and "while the balance of her mind was disturbed by reason of the fact that she had not fully recovered from the eff ect of giving birth", should not be found guilty of murder. But despite this Act, many mothers have been found guilty over the recent years. Around 20 cases per year are reported in the UK.

stem: Which of the following is true for female off enders?
options: More likely than males to off end against family members
Less likely to have a psychiatric disposal
Less likely to self harm than men
ences are more common than crimes of passion
correctAnswer: More likely than males to off end against family members
explanation: The index off ence in women is more likely to be 'romantic' or domestic disputes. 68% of women are in prison for non-violent off ences (compared with 47% for men). Victims of womens' violent acts are more likely to be family members.

stem: In females, which of the following age group is associated with the highest risk of committing a homicide?
explanation: 11% of homicide off enders are women. More than 40% of them fall within the age group 30 to 39 years. The most common victims of female homicide perpetrators are partners (32%) or son/daughters (30%). Strangers constitute less than 5% of victims killed by female homicide off enders.

erence between pleading guilty vs. not guilty.

explanation: Pritchard criteria include 1. Ability to understand charges. 2. Ability to follow proceedings 3. Ability to instruct counsel. 4. Ability to understand the diff erence between pleading guilty vs. not guilty. 5. Ability to challenge juror.

stem: You are seeing a 10-year-old boy with a moderate degree of Learning Disability, microcephaly and self-injurious behavior. The most probable diagnosis is
explanation: Cornelia De Lange syndrome is one among the causes of learning disability due to lack of pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPPA) linked to chromosome 9q33. Clinical features include Continuous eyebrows, hypertrichosis, thin down turning upper lip, Prominent philtrum, small upturned nose, down turned mouth, anteverted nostrils, high arched palate and low set ears, Microcephaly, short stature, small hands and feet, malformed upper limbs, failure to thrive. Behavioural features include self-injury, limited speech in severe cases, language delays, avoidance of being held and stereotypic movements.

stem: According to offi cial crime records, which of the following off ences is most commonly committed by people with autistic spectrum disorder?
explanation: People with autistic spectrum disorders are more likely to commitfi re-setting and other property-damaging off ences. The off ences are usually a result of poor social skills, co-morbid mental health problems, abuse of drugs and alcohol, or because of their narrow stereotyped interests.

stem: Which of the following is a common feature of fragile-x syndrome?
explanation: Fragile X speech is often described as "cluttered". Poor topic maintenance with frequent tangential comments may occur. Syntax is usually appropriate for mental age; a high receptive vocabulary score is usually seen, and auditory sensory and processing skills are weak.

stem: The incidence of fetal alcohol syndrome is;
explanation: The worldwide incidence of the fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) is 1.9 per 1000 live births. Incidence rates vary considerably, however, depending on the study site. Mental retardation is a cardinal feature of FAS and is now recognized as the leading known cause of mental retardation in the Western world. (Ref: Incidence of fetal alcohol syndrome and economic impact of FAS-related anomalies, Abel EL, Sokol RJ)

erent socioeconomic groups of the population

stem: A 62-year-old man has early signs of dementia. Which of the following suggests a cortical rather than a subcortical origin?
explanation: Normal alertness is seen in people with cortical dementia like Alzheimer's disease. 'Slowed up' alertness is seen in people with subcortical dementia like Huntington's disease. Other features of subcortical dementia include impaired attention, impaired executive function, apathetic & inert personality. Normal praxis is a feature of sub cortical dementia whereas apraxia is seen in cortical dementia. (Ref: Seminars in Liaison Psychiatry; 2nd edition: pg 170)

stem: What is the most common medication used for treating patients with Lewy body dementia and psychosis?
explanation: Thefi rst line management of cognitive impairment, psychosis and agitation of Lewy body dementia (DLB) and Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) is a cholinesterase inhibitor (ChEI). In a large RCT, Rivastigmine alleviated visual hallucinations, delusions, anxiety and apathy in DLB (McKeith et al 2006). Levodopa induced hallucinations are also less common when ChEIs are co-prescribed. There is a risk of neuroleptic sensitivity even with atypical antipsychotics of which there are no placebo-controlled trials in DLB. (Ref: Oxford Textbook of Old Age Psychiatry- pg457)

stem: The most common behavioural symptom in Alzheimer's disease is;
explanation: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) refer to the often distressing non-cognitive symptoms of dementia and include agitation and aggressive behaviour. 96% of the patients displayed at least one symptom. Among them, apathy (59.6%) and depression (58.5%) were the most common abnormalities, followed by irritability (44.6%), anxiety (44%) and agitation (41.5%). (Ref: Clustering of behavioural and psychological symptoms in dementia (BPSD): a European Alzheimer's disease consortium (EADC) study-Acta clin Beg- 2007 Nov-Dec;62(6):426-32.)

stem: The drug licensed in UK for the treatments of behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) is
explanation: Risperidone is the only drug licensed in UK for BPSD. It is indicated for the short-term treatment (up to 6 weeks) of persistent aggression in patients with moderate to severe dementia unresponsive to non-pharmacological approaches and when there is a risk of self-harm or others. (Ref: The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry- 11th edition- 509)

stem: Lucy's father has been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease in his 80s. What is the increased risk for her to develop Alzheimer's disease when compared to someone without a positive family history?
explanation: An actual predicted risk of developing Alzheimer's disease in thefi rst-degree relatives of probands with Alzheimer's disease is 15-19%, compared with 5% in controls. "Thus, the risk to thefi rst-degree relatives of patients with Alzheimer's disease who developed the disorder at any time up to the age of 85 years is increased some 3 – 4 times relative to the risk in controls. This would seem to translate to a risk of developing Alzheimer's disease of between one infi ve and one in six". (Excerpt from Liddell et al. (2001) Genetic risk of Alzheimer's disease: advising relatives. The British Journal of Psychiatry, 178, 7-11)

stem: In mild cognitive impairment the best method among those listed here to prevent progression to dementia is
options: Cognitively active lifestyle and brain training
correctAnswer: Cognitively active lifestyle and brain training
explanation: In terms of mild cognitive impairment (MCI), there has been much interest in cognitive training, since low educational ability and reduced engagement in mentally stimulating activities has been shown in population studies to be a predictor of subsequent dementia. Cognitive training strategies have been shown to have some benefi ts with normal older people with MCI, though not yet in randomized controlled trials (so the evidence base is very thin, nevertheless better than others listed). Other management strategies for those with MCI are largely based on knowledge of risk factors and consist of treatment of concurrent disorders, control of vascular risk factors and advice & support regarding cognitive diffi culties. Based on the available data, the use of acetyl cholinesterase inhibitors to delay the onset of Alzheimer's disease cannot be recommended. An expanding literature supports the hypothesis that a cognitively, physically and socially active life style in late life may reduce the risk for Alzheimer's disease. Ginkgo appears ineff ective as a primary preventive measure. (Ref: Oxford textbook of old age psychiatry-413)

stem: Choose the condition that has no clear association with suicide in older people?
explanation: There is no clear association between dementia and suicide in older people. Males are 3-4 times more likely to commit suicide. Depressive illness has been reported in at least 2/3rds of completed suicides in older people. Physical illness, if painful and alcohol abuse are other risk factors for suicide in older people. (Ref: The Oxford Handbook of old age psychiatry- pg 102)

stem: A 77-year-old man with severe dementia has now become psychotic. He is becoming aggressive and distressed due to his psychotic symptoms. He was never before on any antipsychotic medication. Which medication will you use in this situation?
explanation: Risperidone is the only drug licensed for the treatment of BPSD in UK. "It is indicated for the short-term treatment of persistent aggression in patients with moderate to severe Alzheimer's dementia unresponsive to non-pharmacological approaches and when there is a risk of harm to self or others. However, drugs like Drugs Olanzapine and Risperidone should not be routinely used to treat patients with dementia and psychosis unless there is severe distress or a serious risk of physical harm to those living or working with the patients" (Retrieved from http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3549220/). Typical antipsychotics such as haloperidol should not be used in an antipsychotic naive elderly patient due to the risk of developing dystonias and extrapyramidal side eff ects. The evidence for acetyl cholinesterase inhibitors like donepezil in treating BPSD is somewhat inconsistent.

stem: Which one of the following interventions is best proven in RCTs to be eff ective at inducing remission in people with mild to moderate depression?
explanation: Systematic reviews of RCTs involving adults with mild to moderate depression have found that psychological therapies (mainly IPT and cognitive therapy) were more likely to induce remission over ten to 34 weeks than control (usual care, usual care plus placebo pill, or supportive therapy).

stem: A 22-year-old woman diagnosed with bulimia has now relapsed following stressful disputes at the workplace. She has taken to heavy binges and was caught shoplifting at a supermarket. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy?
explanation: Interpersonal therapy (IPT) has been identifi ed as an eff ective treatment for bulimia nervosa that does not focus on bulimic symptoms. Rather, a detailed assessment culminating in a " interpersonal inventory" identifi es core associated interpersonal problem(s) that become the focus of treatment. Hence, IPT may be particularly helpful for clients who have become "stuck" in their eating disorder for reasons associated with problematic relationships. IPT is also helpful for clients who may benefi t from a therapy that off ers some structure, focus, and containment without clear behavioural directives. This may even aid in forming an amicable relationship with professionals involved. Apple, RF. (1999) Interpersonal therapy for bulimia nervosa. Journal of Clinical Psychology, 55, 715-725.

stem: Therapeutic regression is an important component of which of the following psychotherapies?
explanation: Psychoanalysis uses the term therapeutic regression whereby the psychoanalysis itself is considered to induce a regressive state where transference is allowed and then studied.

stem: Harmful emotions and personally dysfunctional behaviours can arise as a result of irrational thinking. This is the rationale behind which of the following psychotherapy?
explanation: Albert Ellis developed Rational Emotive Therapy in 1955. It is a reality-based, short-term therapy aimed at cognitive re-structuring with many similarities of the later developed CBT. The rationale behind this therapy is harmful emotions and personally dysfunctional behaviours can arise as a result of irrational thinking and the therapist uses guided discussion, logic, real-life challenges and appropriate humour to challenge irrational thinking.

stem: A young man, who repetitively fought with his father, stopped visiting him for many years. But after his father's death, he has now decided to look after his father?s business and moved in to live in his father's house to be close to his memory. What is the possible defence mechanism?
explanation: Reaction formation involves transforming an unacceptable impulse into its exact opposite. Reaction formation is characteristic of obsessional neurosis though it occurs in other forms of neuroses too. Repeated use of reaction formation at any early stage of ego development could lead to it becoming a permanent character trait, as in an obsessional personality.

stem: A psychotherapist describes her methods as one that depends on rules about how members of a family relate to each other. This is called
explanation: Families function as an interacting system: what one member does or says infl uences not only other individual members but also the function of the whole family as a group. This is exploited by Systemic Family Therapy.

stem: Massed practice is used as a therapy for which of the following conditions?
explanation: Massed negative practice is one of the most frequently used behavioural techniques in the treatment for tic disorder. The patient is asked to deliberately perform the tic movement for specifi ed periods of time interspersed with brief periods of rest.

stem: A religious man practices celibacy and abstains from all sexual relationships by reason of his religious vows. The defense mechanism used here is
explanation: Asceticism is a mature defense mechanism, which involves the abolition of directly pleasurable events or practices but deriving gratifi cation from the act of renunciation of the desired object. A strong "moral" element is implicit in this defense mechanism.

stem: A psychiatric trainee is providing supervised psychotherapy to a patient. Following assessment by the trainee who is of Indian ethnicity, the patient asks for a transfer to a therapist of her own cultural background. The most appropriate next step for the trainee is to

explanation: It is always prudent to explore the beliefs and values of patients before acting to address them.

stem: Disorders in Liaison Psychiatry (1) As a trainee liaison psychiatrist, you have been asked to see the following patients in a general hospital ward. Select the most appropriate diagnosis, for each of the following presentations: A 47-year-old woman presenting with a 4-year history of multiple vague physical symptoms not explained by any physical causes. She seeks repeated consultations with her GP s and hospital specialists. A 35-year-old gentleman who presents himself 30 miles away from his residence for no apparent reason with well-maintained self-care. When asked how many legs a cat has, a 42-year-old male prisoner answers 'fi ve legs.' Choose... Choose... Choose...
correctAnswer: A 47-year-old woman presenting with a 4-year history of multiple vague physical symptoms not explained by any physical causes. She seeks repeated consultations with her GP s and hospital specialists. → Somatisation disorder, A 35-year-old gentleman who presents himself 30 miles away from his residence for no apparent reason with well-maintained self-care. → Dissociative fugue, When asked how many legs a cat has, a 42-year-old male prisoner answers 'fi ve legs.' → Ganser's syndrome
explanation:
1) Somatisation is the experience of bodily symptoms with no suffi cient physical cause; there is often a presumed psychological cause of these symptoms. In hypochondriasis patient looks for diagnosis, not symptom relief; he/she names a suspected disorder and may be thoroughly convinced about having the disorder. In a patient with somatisation, Musculoskeletal symptoms are common; while in hypochondriasis gastrointestinal problems are the most common ones. Family history of alcohol use and antisocial personality may be more common in women with somatization disorder. 2) Fugue is a type of a dissociative reaction to severe stress. It could happen following a signifi cant external stressor that the aff ected individual develops global amnesia and may wander to a distant location. Consciousness is unimpaired.

3) Ganser syndrome is related to the production of approximate answers. When interviewed, the patient gives answers that are wrong, but nonetheless in the right ballpark. Occasionally this may be associated with organic brain illness; it is much more commonly seen as a form of dissociation or as malingering (e.g. in prisoners awaiting trial)

stem: Personality disorder (6) For each of the traits given below, identify the most appropriate personality disorder in which it is seen. Increased sensitivity to criticisms and setbacks Fear of abandonment and rely on other people Inability to make decisions Strive continuously for perfection Choose... Choose... Choose... Choose...
correctAnswer: Increased sensitivity to criticisms and setbacks → Paranoid personality disorder, Fear of abandonment and rely on other people → Borderline personality disorder, Inability to make decisions → Dependent personality disorder, Strive continuously for perfection → Anankastic personality disorder
explanation:
1) Paranoid personality disorder: Suspicious of other people and their motives, highly sensitive to criticisms and setbacks, hold longstanding grudges against people, believe others are not trustworthy, emotionally detached and feel other people are deceiving, threatening, or making plans against them. 2) Borderline personality disorder: poor self-image, unstable personal relationships, Impulsive behaviour in areas such as personal safety and substance misuse, may self-harm, feel suicidal and act on these feelings, experience instability of mood, Have episodes of micro- psychosis, feelings of chronic emptiness and fears of abandonment - rejection sensitivity hence form intense but short lasting relations. 3) Dependent personality disorder- assumes a position of passivity, Allowing others to take responsibility for most areas of their daily life, lack self-confi dence, feel unable to function independently of another person, Feels own needs are of secondary importance.

4) Obsessive-compulsive (Anankastic) personality disorder- Diffi culties in expressing warm or tender emotions to others, frequently perfectionists, often lack clarity in seeing other perspectives or ways of doing things, Rigid attention to detail may prevent them from completing tasks, Some may be hoarders, excessively scrupulous with money, may not be able to delegate tasks and are often workaholics.

stem: Prevention & types Identify one correct option for each of the following preventive measures in schizophrenia Urban living for schizophrenia Identifi cation of a preschizophrenic state Cannabis and psychosis Environmental adjustments and aids in learning disabled adult. Choose... Choose... Choose... Choose...
correctAnswer: Urban living for schizophrenia → Universal prevention, Identifi cation of a preschizophrenic state → Indicated prevention, Cannabis and psychosis → Selective prevention, Environmental adjustments and aids in learning disabled adult. → Tertiary prevention
explanation: Universal prevention/interventions are directed to a general population group. For schizophrenia, some epidemiological factors such as urban living, poor social capital including low social cohesion, exclusion and discrimination, low socioeconomic status are so widespread that their targeting can be considered a universal intervention. Indicated interventions target high-risk individuals with minimal but detectable signs or symptoms foreshadowing mental disorder, but who do not meet diagnostic levels e.g identifi cation of a preschizophrenic state/prodrome of schizophrenia. Selective interventions are targeted to individuals or subgroups whose risk of developing disorder is signifi cantly higher than average. Perinatal complications and cannabis use have stimulated interest as a putative risk factors for schizophrenia. Both selective and indicated approaches are secondary prevention methods. Tertiary prevention helps an individual to attain his or her full developmental potential through rehabilitation, which includes education, support, environmental adjustments and aids.
